changelog.change: Initial entry — adult DKA/HHS diagnostic criteria, severity grading, the fluid / potassium / insulin sequence, adjuncts (bicarbonate, phosphate), euglycemic DKA, resolution and IV-to-SC transition. Adult counterpart to peds-dka-management (cross-linked).

summary: Fluids first, then potassium, then insulin — in that order. DKA is an insulin-deficiency + ketoacid problem (fix the gap); HHS is a profound free-water deficit with little ketosis (fluid does most of the work, insulin is gentler). The number that kills is potassium: check it before the first unit of insulin, and never run insulin with a K < 3.3 mEq/L.
whyThisMatters: Both present as sick, dry, hyperglycaemic patients, and the reflex — a big insulin bolus — is exactly wrong until you have a potassium and a litre of saline running. Insulin drives K intracellularly; a normal or low serum K at presentation is already a large total-body deficit, and pushing insulin into it causes the arrhythmia that turns a treatable metabolic emergency into an arrest. The other trap is stopping too early: normalising the glucose is not the endpoint — the anion gap (DKA) or the osmolality and mental status (HHS) are.
clinicalTakeaway: Start 0.9% saline ~15-20 mL/kg (about 1 L) in the first hour while the labs run. Check potassium immediately: K < 3.3 → hold insulin and replace K 10-20 mEq/h until ≥ 3.3; K 3.3-5.2 → add 20-30 mEq K to each litre and keep it 4-5; K > 5.2 → insulin without added K, recheck in 2 h. Then regular insulin 0.1 unit/kg/h IV (a 0.1 unit/kg bolus is optional; skip it and use 0.14 unit/kg/h if you prefer). Add dextrose to the fluids once glucose falls below ~200 mg/dL (DKA) or ~250-300 (HHS) and keep the insulin running until the anion gap has closed / β-hydroxybutyrate < 0.6 mmol/L — then overlap subcutaneous insulin by 1-2 h before stopping the drip. Give bicarbonate only for a pH < 6.9. Always look for and treat the precipitant.

rows: > 250 mg/dL (may be < 250 — euglycemic DKA, esp. SGLT2 inhibitor, pregnancy, poor intake, alcohol)

body.text: Overlap is common — up to a third of hyperglycaemic crises are mixed DKA + HHS. Treat the acidosis as DKA and the osmolar/volume deficit as HHS. Use a POC β-hydroxybutyrate if available; urine ketones (acetoacetate) lag and can paradoxically rise as the patient improves.

Severe DKA, HHS, haemodynamic instability, a depressed conscious level, or a difficult airway → ICU / high-dependency care. JBDS markers of severity also include β-hydroxybutyrate > 6 mmol/L, GCS < 12, SpO₂ < 92%, SBP < 90, pulse > 100 or < 60, and a potassium < 3.5 on admission.

items: Isotonic crystalloid: 0.9% sodium chloride (balanced solutions such as Plasma-Lyte / Ringer's lactate are a reasonable alternative and may close the gap slightly faster with less hyperchloraemia).
First hour: ~15-20 mL/kg (roughly 1 L in an average adult), faster and repeated for shock.
Then ~250-500 mL/h, titrated to volume status, urine output, and the corrected sodium. Switch to 0.45% NaCl if the corrected Na is normal or high; stay on 0.9% if it is low.
Total deficit is large — DKA ~100 mL/kg (~6 L), HHS ~100-220 mL/kg (~8-10 L). Replace over ~24 h in DKA and more slowly in HHS to avoid dropping the osmolality faster than ~3 mOsm/kg/h.

Add dextrose (D5W, or D10W if the glucose is falling fast) to the running fluid once glucose < ~200 mg/dL in DKA or < ~250-300 mg/dL in HHS, so the insulin can keep clearing ketones without hypoglycaemia.

rows: HOLD insulin. Give 10-20 mEq/h IV potassium (with cardiac monitoring) until K ≥ 3.3, then start insulin.
Start insulin AND add 20-30 mEq K⁺ to each litre of fluid; target serum K⁺ 4-5. Recheck every 2-4 h.
Start insulin, no potassium yet. Recheck K⁺ in 2 h and add it once it falls below 5.2.

body.text: Every DKA/HHS patient has a whole-body potassium deficit (typically 3-5 mEq/kg) even when the serum level is normal or high — insulin, fluids, and correction of acidosis all drive K⁺ back into cells. Anticipate the fall. Replace phosphate only if PO₄ < 1 mg/dL with cardiac dysfunction, respiratory depression, or haemolytic anaemia (then some of the K⁺ can be given as potassium phosphate); routine phosphate repletion has no benefit and risks hypocalcaemia.

items: Regular (short-acting) insulin by IV infusion. Either: 0.1 unit/kg IV bolus then 0.1 unit/kg/h; or no bolus and 0.14 unit/kg/h — equivalent outcomes.
Aim for a glucose fall of 50-75 mg/dL/h. If it has not dropped by ≥ 10% (or ~50 mg/dL) in the first hour, re-bolus 0.1 unit/kg or double the infusion — after confirming fluids are actually running.
Once dextrose is added, keep the insulin at ~0.05-0.1 unit/kg/h and titrate the dextrose (and rate) to hold glucose ~150-200 mg/dL (DKA) / ~250-300 (HHS) while the gap closes.
HHS: insulin is an adjunct — start lower (~0.05 unit/kg/h) or even fluid-only initially; the glucose falls with rehydration alone and an aggressive drip drops the osmolality too fast.
Subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin every 1-2 h is an option for MILD, uncomplicated DKA on a ward with close monitoring — not for moderate/severe DKA or HHS.

Do NOT stop the infusion when the glucose normalises. Continue until DKA has resolved, then overlap a long-acting SC insulin dose and wait 1-2 h before discontinuing the drip (no overlap = rebound ketoacidosis). Continue the patient's usual basal insulin throughout if they were already on it.
Bicarbonate: only for pH < 6.9 — 100 mmol NaHCO₃ in 400 mL water with 20 mEq KCl over 2 h, repeat until pH ≥ 7.0. No proven benefit at pH ≥ 6.9 and it worsens hypokalaemia and CSF acidosis.
VTE prophylaxis: pharmacologic unless contraindicated (HHS in particular is highly prothrombotic).

Identify and treat the precipitant: infection (the commonest — culture and consider empiric antibiotics if febrile/toxic), missed insulin or pump failure, new-onset diabetes, acute MI or stroke, pancreatitis, pregnancy, and drugs — corticosteroids, SGLT2 inhibitors (euglycemic DKA), atypical antipsychotics, sympathomimetics, high-dose thiazides.
Hold SGLT2 inhibitors; they can sustain ketogenesis for days after the last dose, so continue the insulin + dextrose infusion longer and confirm ketone clearance by β-hydroxybutyrate, not glucose.
Bedside glucose hourly.
Venous blood gas / electrolytes / anion gap (and β-hydroxybutyrate if available) at 2 h, then every 2-4 h until the gap has closed.
Continuous cardiac monitoring while replacing potassium.

Hourly fluid balance; watch for fluid overload (elderly, cardiac/renal disease) and, in the young, for cerebral oedema (headache, falling GCS, bradycardia + hypertension — far more common in children; see peds-dka-management).
DKA resolved: glucose < 200 mg/dL AND two of — bicarbonate ≥ 15 mEq/L, venous pH > 7.3, anion gap ≤ 12 mEq/L. (β-hydroxybutyrate < 0.6 mmol/L is the cleanest single marker where available.)
HHS resolved: effective osmolality normalising, normal mental status, and adequate urine output — this takes longer, often 24-48 h.

Transition: when the patient is eating and DKA has resolved, give the first SC dose (their home regimen, or ~0.5-0.6 unit/kg/day insulin-naïve, split basal/bolus) and continue the IV infusion for another 1-2 h. An endocrine / diabetes team review before discharge reduces readmission.

buildNote: Tier 2 — the fluid/potassium/insulin doctrine is stable; the euglycemic-DKA / SGLT2 guidance and the move toward balanced crystalloids and POC ketones are the parts to re-check (2024 ADA/EASD/AACE consensus). Adult counterpart to peds-dka-management, which is cross-listed into Reference Library / Critical Care to sit beside this. Numeric ranges are order-of-magnitude starting points, not a substitute for a local DKA/HHS protocol.
